0.title: The Kinsman-Redeemer: The Book of Ruth
0.overview:
The message. Ruth shows God quietly at work for people who cannot see him. In one of Israel’s darkest ages a widow loses everything and comes home saying, “I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty” (1:21). Through a foreign daughter-in-law who will not leave her, and a kinsman who chooses to redeem them at his own cost, God fills her again, and from that small household he brings Israel its king. The thread through it all is the LORD’s steadfast love, his faithful kindness to people who have no claim on him. There are no miracles and God speaks no word, yet the whole story is in his hands, and it ends at the cradle of David and, beyond him, of David’s greater Son.

Background: when and where. The story is set “in the days when the judges ruled” (1:1), after Joshua and before Israel had a king. The book of Judges sums up that age in its last line: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). If Obed was David’s grandfather, the events fall about 1100 BC. The family comes from Bethlehem, whose name means “house of bread”, yet there is famine in it, and they cross to Moab, east of the Dead Sea. Moab was descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36–37), worshipped the god Chemosh, and had long been Israel’s enemy. Even the names tell the story: Elimelech, “my God is king”, in an age without a king; Naomi, “pleasant”, who asks to be called Mara, “bitter” (1:20).

The writer and the date. The book does not name its author. The Talmud credited Samuel, but the book seems to look back from a later time: it explains a custom “in former times in Israel” (4:7), and its closing genealogy reaches David. Because it stops at David, not Solomon, many conservative scholars place it in or soon after David’s reign. Many modern scholars date it after the exile, as a gentle protest against the ban on foreign wives under Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 10; Nehemiah 13:1–3). But the book has no air of controversy, and its interest is in the house of David rather than the returned exiles. This commentary takes it to have been written under the monarchy, leaving the exact date open; its lesson stands either way.

The kind of writing. Ruth is history, told as a short story with great art, its scenes balanced and its key words echoing across chapters. Matthew writes Ruth into the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The Hebrew Bible places it among the Writings, where in many printings it follows Proverbs, whose last chapter praises “an excellent wife” (Proverbs 31:10): Boaz calls Ruth “a worthy woman” (3:11), the same phrase in Hebrew. Jewish custom reads it at the Feast of Weeks, the end of the grain harvest. English Bibles follow the Greek order and set it after Judges, a bright window in a dark wall. Read it slowly, and watch for what the narrator does not say: Ruth “happened” to come to the field of Boaz (2:3), and the reader is meant to smile.

The world of the book. Three customs carry the plot. Israel’s law told farmers to leave the edges of their fields and the dropped grain for the poor, the widow and the foreigner, and Ruth is all three. The law also gave the role of redeemer (go’el) to a near relative, who had the right and duty to buy back family land sold in poverty (Leviticus 25:25) and to rescue a kinsman sold into slavery. And a dead man’s brother was to marry his childless widow to raise up an heir in his name (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). Ruth’s night visit to the threshing floor is an appeal to these duties, and the matter is settled before the elders at the city gate, where a drawn-off sandal sealed the transfer (4:7).

How the book makes its case. The story moves from emptiness to fullness in four scenes. Emptied (chapter 1): famine and three deaths strip Naomi bare, but at the crossroads Ruth binds herself to her with an oath: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (1:16). They reach Bethlehem “at the beginning of barley harvest” (1:22). Provided for (chapter 2): gleaning in the field of Boaz, Ruth is protected and fed beyond the law’s demand, and he blesses her by “the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (2:12). The appeal (chapter 3): at the threshing floor Ruth asks Boaz, “Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer” (3:9), and he becomes the answer to his own prayer. Redeemed (chapter 4): the nearer kinsman draws back, “lest I impair my own inheritance” (4:6); Boaz pays the cost, marries Ruth, and “the LORD gave her conception” (4:13). The women set the child in Naomi’s lap and bless the LORD, “who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (4:14). The genealogy (4:18–22) sets the village story in the history of salvation.

A Moabite in Israel? How could this be, when the law said, “No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 23:3). Some Jewish teachers read the law as applying to Moabite men, but the book’s own answer lies in Ruth’s vow. Moab was shut out for its hostility to God’s people and its gods; Ruth left both and took the LORD as her God. Orpah went back “to her people and to her gods” (1:15); Ruth came, like Rahab before her, by faith. This commentary’s view is that the law was never a wall against a foreigner who truly turned to the LORD, and that Ruth’s welcome shows the reach of his grace.

Where it leads: to Christ. Ruth points to Christ by his family line, by pattern, and by the character of God it shows. First the line: Obed was the grandfather of David, and Matthew names “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5) in the genealogy of Jesus, beside Tamar and Rahab, outsiders brought in by grace. Bethlehem, the house of bread, became the town of the Messiah (Micah 5:2; Luke 2:4). Then the pattern: the New Testament never names Boaz as a picture of Christ, but it calls Christ our Redeemer and shows him becoming our kinsman: “Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things” (Hebrews 2:14), and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). The nearer kinsman would not risk his inheritance; Christ, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and paid the price of our redemption “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19). And the wings: Ruth sought refuge under God’s wings, and Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem “as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Matthew 23:37). The likeness lies in the redeemer’s right, cost and willing heart; the barley and the sandal belong to the story and are not hidden symbols.

For us. Ruth teaches us to trust God when he is hidden. God answers Naomi’s honest bitterness not with rebuke but with a harvest and a grandson. The book also calls us to live out the loyal love we have received: to stay when leaving would be easier, to give more than duty asks, and to welcome the outsider, for in Christ “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). Above all it shows us a Redeemer who had the right, paid the cost and was willing, and who will not leave his people empty.

1.title: Emptied and Returning
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons.<sup>2</sup>The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there.<sup>3</sup>But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons.<sup>4</sup>These took Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years,<sup>5</sup>and both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband.<sup>6</sup>Then she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited his people and given them food.<sup>7</sup>So she set out from the place where she was with her two daughters-in-law, and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah.<sup>8</sup>But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.<sup>9</sup>The LORD grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!" Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept.<sup>10</sup>And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people."<sup>11</sup>But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why will you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb that they may become your husbands?<sup>12</sup>Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. If I should say I have hope, even if I should have a husband this night and should bear sons,<sup>13</sup>would you therefore wait till they were grown? Would you therefore refrain from marrying? No, my daughters, for it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."<sup>14</sup>Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her.<sup>15</sup>And she said, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law."<sup>16</sup>But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.<sup>17</sup>Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you."<sup>18</sup>And when Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more.<sup>19</sup>So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. And the women said, "Is this Naomi?"<sup>20</sup>She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.<sup>21</sup>I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?"<sup>22</sup>So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest.
1.overview:
Where we are. Ruth opens “in the days when the judges ruled” (v. 1), the darkest stretch of Israel’s life in the land, when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). This chapter is the first of the book’s four scenes: the emptying of a family from Bethlehem.

The message. God does not abandon his people when he empties them; he is at work in the loss before anyone can see it. Naomi loses husband, sons and future, and says honestly that the LORD has done it. She is right that his hand is in it, and wrong that it is against her. For beside her walks a Moabite widow who has sworn herself to Naomi’s God, and the chapter ends with the barley harvest beginning.

Why it was said. The book was written for Israel under the house of David (see the introduction). It shows them that their royal line began in a widow’s emptiness and a foreigner’s faith, and teaches every believer who feels the LORD’s hand “gone out against me” (v. 13) that God works through famine, funerals and silence as surely as through miracles.

How the chapter makes its case. Famine drives a Bethlehem family to Moab, where a short stay becomes ten years and three funerals, and Naomi is left as simply “the woman” (vv. 1–5). When the LORD visits his people with food, she turns for home and presses her daughters-in-law to go back; Orpah goes “to her people and to her gods”, but Ruth clings to Naomi and swears herself to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God until death (vv. 6–18). In Bethlehem Naomi asks to be called Mara, “bitter”, for the Almighty has brought her back empty; but the narrator’s last words are “the beginning of barley harvest” (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by pattern. The chapter leaves a family line cut off and a widow with no one to redeem her; the rest of the book answers that need, and the answer leads to David and his greater Son. And Ruth’s vow is a small human likeness of the loyal love God shows in Christ, who left his home, went where we go, took our people as his own and died our death, so that he can say, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

For us. Bring your bitterness to God as Naomi did; he can bear honest lament. But do not read your losses as his verdict on you, for at the cross that verdict has already been given. And ask Ruth’s question: is the LORD your God when following him costs you everything else?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Family Emptied in Moab
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Over ten years in Moab a family is emptied of its future, and the narrator tells it without comment. Famine drives Elimelech, Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem, the “house of bread”, across the border to Moab (vv. 1–2), and a short stay becomes a settled life. Elimelech dies (v. 3); the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and after about ten years both sons die childless (vv. 4–5). Naomi is left as simply “the woman”, without husband, sons or heir, and Elimelech’s line seems to be at an end. Yet the story is already in God’s hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verses set the book's tension between fullness and emptiness and raise the hard question of how God rules over suffering. The narrator does not explicitly condemn the move to Moab, but three funerals in five verses cast a shadow. Moab was a dangerous place for Israel’s faith (Num 25). Yet God's sovereignty stands over the whole episode; even the deaths that empty Naomi are dark threads from which he will weave redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi's family did what families have always done in crisis: they sought survival wherever it could be found, even at the cost of leaving the covenant land and people. Ruth offers no cheap answers to why God's people suffer. It shows a family in ruins, and asks the grieving reader only to keep reading.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days when the judges ruled there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the darkest age of Israel’s life in the land, famine drives a Bethlehem family across the border into Moab, and the story of redemption begins in emptiness.

In the days when the judges ruled. The age summed up as “everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25; see the introduction). In that darkness God works this jewel of a story.

There was a famine in the land. A stinging irony: Bethlehem means “house of bread”, and there is no bread. Famine in the land of promise was one of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28), though the narrator does not say this one was a punishment.

To sojourn in the country of Moab. To live there as foreigners for a while. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a few days’ walk away, good grain and grazing country that a famine in Judah did not necessarily reach. Its people were descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36–37), worshipped Chemosh, and had long been Israel’s enemy.

Was the move to Moab a sin? The text does not condemn it outright; Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had all gone abroad in famine. But a short stay became a settled home (v. 2), and the sons married Moabite women. The drift away from the land of promise is the quiet warning. Yet God governs even the wanderings of those who stray, and Moab will become the soil where faith blooms.
verseByVerse.note: Ruth is set in the time of the judges, before Israel had a king.

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the man was Elimelech and the name of his wife Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went into the country of Moab and remained there. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family’s names speak, and the last words of the verse tell how a temporary refuge became a settled home.

The name of the man was Elimelech. Elimelech means “my God is king”, yet its bearer leaves the land where God reigns. Naomi means “pleasant”, a name she will renounce in her bitterness (v. 20). Mahlon and Chilion sound like words for sickness and wasting away, names that whisper of the deaths to come.

Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. An established clan of the town, from the Ephrathah out of which, Micah would say, Israel’s ruler was to come (Micah 5:2).

And remained there. Quietly damning: a sojourn becomes a settled life. Compromise rarely comes as one decisive rebellion; more often it is a gradual settling into a place we were never meant to stay. But the narrator never says that the deaths that follow were the price of it, and neither should we.
verseByVerse.note: Ephrath was an older name for the Bethlehem area (Gen 35:19).

verseByVerse.quote: But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died, and she was left with her two sons. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi’s husband dies in a foreign land, and her whole future now hangs on two sons.

But Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died. The first blow, in a few plain words.

She was left with her two sons. From here the story is told from Naomi’s side: “she was left”, a survivor being stripped of her family. A widow’s security lay in her husband and then in her sons.

God’s hand in it. Providence, God’s rule over all that happens, does not make God the author of evil, but it does mean that nothing, not even bereavement in a foreign land, falls outside his governance. Naomi cannot yet see it, but he is at work in her loss.

Grief told honestly. Scripture does not airbrush what God’s people endure, and neither need we, in our prayers or with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: These took Moabite wives; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years, and both Mahlon and Chilion died, so that the woman was left without her two sons and her husband. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons marry Moabite women and then die childless, leaving Naomi alone and Elimelech’s line apparently ended.

These took Moabite wives. Women of a nation the law kept out of Israel’s assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3), and in ten years no children. Here we first meet Orpah and Ruth.

Both Mahlon and Chilion died. In the last clause Naomi is not even named; she is simply “the woman”, stripped of husband, sons and any heir to carry the name. Humanly speaking, this is a dead end. Yet God characteristically works through emptiness and impossibility, so that the redemption will be unmistakably his, the pattern he follows to the end, when life comes out of a grave.

Was it wrong to marry Moabite women? The law forbade marriage with the Canaanites (Deuteronomy 7:3), not expressly with Moabites, but it warned of foreign wives turning hearts to their gods (1 Kings 11:1–2). The real issue was faith: Orpah went back to her gods (v. 15); Ruth turned to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–18 — The Crossroads: Orpah's Return and Ruth's Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road between Moab and Judah, two daughters-in-law choose between their old gods and the LORD. Hearing that the LORD has visited his people with food, Naomi sets out for home (vv. 6–7). She blesses Orpah and Ruth and urges them to go back and find husbands, arguing that she has nothing left to give them and that the LORD’s hand is against her (vv. 8–13). Orpah kisses her goodbye and returns “to her people and to her gods”; Ruth clings to Naomi (vv. 14–15) and binds herself by oath to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God until death (vv. 16–17). Naomi says no more (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: This section turns on hesed. Naomi invokes it as a prayer over her daughters-in-law (v. 8), and Ruth embodies it in her vow: grace producing faith, and faith producing costly loyalty.
verseByVerse.examples: The fork in the road tests every relationship. Orpah's choice is reasonable by ordinary standards; Ruth's is extravagant and risky. Covenant love is proven not when staying is easy but when leaving would be sensible. Ruth shows a discipleship that counts the cost and follows anyway, the kind Jesus would later ask of his followers, and she can choose it because the God whose hesed she has seen in Naomi's house has first drawn her to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she arose with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard in the fields of Moab that the LORD had visited his people and given them food. So she set out from the place where she was with her two daughters-in-law, and they went on the way to return to the land of Judah. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Naomi hears that the LORD has given his people food again, she sets out for home, and God’s kindness begins to draw her back.

The LORD had visited his people. The first ray of light. “Visited” (paqad) is used when God remembers his promises and steps in with mercy (Genesis 50:24; Exodus 4:31). Only here and in 4:13 (“the LORD gave her conception”) does the narrator himself say the LORD did something; the two acts frame the story: food for the land, a child for the family.

To return. “Return” (shub) sounds again and again through the chapter, with the double sense of homecoming and repentance. God’s mercy to Bethlehem reaches into “the fields of Moab” to draw his people home, and the harvest that feeds Bethlehem will bring Ruth to the field of Boaz (2:3). Naomi sees only the long road back; God is leading her into the centre of his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, return each of you to her mother's house. May the LORD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. The LORD grant that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband!" Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi releases her daughters-in-law with a blessing, praying that the LORD will repay their kindness with a home.

May the LORD deal kindly with you. Naomi’s first recorded words are a blessing. “Deal kindly” uses hesed, the loyal love beyond duty that the Old Testament most often ascribes to God himself: may his hesed repay theirs to the dead and to her. Desolate herself, she still believes God is kind, though she can no longer feel that he is kind to her.

That you may find rest. A settled home in a husband’s house, a widow’s only security in that world. Naomi urges away the only companions she has left, seeking their good above her own. Her prayer is more prophetic than she knows: she will seek “rest” for Ruth herself (3:1), and God will give it in the house of a redeemer and in the line of the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people." But Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters; why will you go with me? Have I yet sons in my womb that they may become your husbands? Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to have a husband. If I should say I have hope, even if I should have a husband this night and should bear sons, would you therefore wait till they were grown? Would you therefore refrain from marrying? No, my daughters, for it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake that the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi argues that she has nothing left to offer them, and traces her losses to the LORD’s own hand. At first both young women refuse to leave her (v. 10).

Have I yet sons in my womb? She appeals to the custom by which a dead man’s brother married his childless widow to raise up an heir (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). She has no more sons, and even if she bore some, the young women could not wait for them to grow up. The airtight logic is meant to release them from any obligation.

The hand of the LORD has gone out against me. She blames not fate, chance or Moab but the LORD. Naomi never doubts God’s sovereignty; she struggles to reconcile it with his goodness. She is wrong that his hand is against her (it is secretly for her), but right that his hand is in it all. This is the lament of faith, still addressing its complaint to God (compare Psalm 88), and there is more faith in it than in many a placid contentment.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “it is exceedingly bitter to me for your sake” is compressed: it may mean that she grieves for them, or (as several translations take it) that her lot is more bitter than theirs, since they can remarry and she cannot. Either way she sees herself as the one the LORD has struck.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they lifted up their voices and wept again. And Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her. And she said, "See, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods; return after your sister-in-law." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two daughters-in-law part ways: Orpah kisses Naomi goodbye and goes home, while Ruth clings to her.

They lifted up their voices and wept again. The hinge of the chapter, where two lives divide.

Orpah kissed her mother-in-law. A loving farewell. We should not despise Orpah: hers is the reasonable choice, the one Naomi urged.

But Ruth clung to her. The verb (dabaq) is the word of Genesis 2:24 for a man holding fast to his wife, and of Deuteronomy for Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20): a lasting, covenantal joining.

To her people and to her gods. The phrase exposes the stakes. To go back to Moab is to go back to Chemosh, its god; to stay with Naomi is to embrace the LORD. Orpah chose the safe and calculable; Ruth, the costly commitment of faith that will lose everything to gain the one thing needful.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ruth said, "Do not urge me to leave you or to return from following you. For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried. May the LORD do so to me and more also if anything but death parts me from you." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth binds herself by oath to Naomi, to her people and to her God for the rest of her life: this is a Moabite’s conversion.

Do not urge me to leave you. Her words rise line on line: where you go, where you lodge, your people, your God, where you die. She binds herself not only to a person but to a people and, above all, to a God.

Your God my God. The moment of conversion: a Moabite raised on Chemosh casts herself wholly on the LORD, and follows a bitter, empty old woman towards poverty to do it. This is hesed in its purest human form, mirroring the hesed of God himself.

May the LORD do so to me and more also. An oath in the covenant name of Israel’s God, calling down his judgment on herself if anything but death parts them.

A small copy of something larger. Ruth’s vow anticipates the gospel: the outsider drawn by grace into the covenant, firstfruits of the nations who will say of Israel’s God, “this is God, our God forever and ever” (Psalm 48:14). And it is a small human copy of a far greater faithfulness. God did not keep his options open with us. He bound himself by covenant, and in Christ he went where we go, lodged where we lodge, and died our death, so that he could say, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Only people held like that can afford to make promises like hers.

Why not keep your options open? Orpah’s choice is the one our culture understands best: commit too soon, to a person, a place or a faith, and you may miss something better. Yet the psychologist Barry Schwartz has argued that endless choice does not make us happier; past a point it leaves us anxious, second-guessing and less content with whatever we chose. A self that never binds itself never quite becomes anyone. Ruth does the reverse. She closes every door but one, and the one she walks through leads into a people and a God.

Words read at weddings. These words are often read at weddings. They were spoken by a daughter-in-law to her mother-in-law, not by a bride; but they describe the costly, lifelong loyalty marriage requires, so the use is a fair one by application.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she said no more. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing that Ruth cannot be moved, Naomi stops arguing, and the bond between them is sealed in silence.

She was determined. Literally, she had made herself strong.

She said no more. The silence may carry a trace of Naomi’s numbness, perhaps even reluctance at one more mouth to feed; in Bethlehem she will not mention Ruth at all (v. 21). Yet it also marks acceptance. What Naomi cannot yet grasp is that the companion she could not dissuade is the one God will use to fill her emptiness, the great-grandmother of King David.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — Empty in Bethlehem, Yet the Harvest Begins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Naomi comes home empty and says so, but the narrator ends with a harvest. The whole town of Bethlehem is stirred, and the women ask, “Is this Naomi?” (v. 19). She tells them to call her Mara, “bitter”, for the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her: she went away full and the LORD has brought her back empty (vv. 20–21). Her lament is honest and her belief in God’s rule is intact, but she has misread his purpose and overlooked the daughter-in-law beside her. The last line sets the two women in Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest (v. 22), where God is already preparing to fill her.
verseByVerse.theology: Naomi brings her wound to God rather than away from him. Her lament is faith, though her reading of it is incomplete, and the closing note of barley harvest is the quiet voice of providence.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi says her grief aloud, to God and to her neighbours, and Scripture keeps her words; a church that makes room for lament is following her example. And the barley harvest is a reminder that the seasons of God's mercy often begin precisely when our hope is at its lowest.

verseByVerse.quote: So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they came to Bethlehem, the whole town was stirred because of them. And the women said, "Is this Naomi?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole town is stirred at Naomi’s return, for sorrow has so changed her that the women can hardly believe it is she.

The whole town was stirred. The woman who left a decade ago, wife and mother, comes back aged by grief with only a Moabite widow beside her.

Is this Naomi? Half recognition, half disbelief: suffering can change a person until old neighbours scarcely know her.

Empty at harvest time. She comes back empty just as the harvest comes in (v. 22): the homecoming that looks like the end of a tragedy is the opening of redemption. The same women will gather again in chapter 4, to bless the LORD over Naomi’s grandson (4:14–17).

verseByVerse.quote: She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi renames herself “Bitter” and says plainly that the Almighty has emptied her; her lament is honest, but it is not the last word.

Call me Mara. She rejects “Naomi” (pleasant) for “Mara” (bitter). Four times in two verses she names God as the author of her affliction: no unbeliever’s complaint, but a believer who knows nothing happens outside his hand.

The LORD has brought me back empty. Yet she reads her emptiness as God’s verdict against her (“the LORD has testified against me”, the language of a witness in court). And she says “empty” while Ruth stands beside her: the one through whom God will fill her is the one she does not count.

The Almighty. Naomi’s word for God here is Shaddai, the name under which God promised the patriarchs children and a future: “I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 35:11). That is what makes her sentence so bitter: the God of fruitfulness has left her empty. In pain we either shrink God, so that he is not responsible, or keep him large and decide he is against us. Naomi does the second. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a God great enough to be blamed for our suffering is also great enough to have reasons for it that we cannot yet see. See also Omnipotence in the Theological Dictionary.

The verdict already given. We see what Naomi could not. Jesus was emptied, and on the cross drank the bitterness that should have been ours, so the verdict on everyone who trusts him is settled: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

In everyday life. We are poor judges of our own circumstances. God can bear honest lament; whole psalms are made of it. When loss comes, say Naomi’s words to him if you must. But do not read the loss as his verdict on you; the cross has already given that.

Uncertain wording. The origin of Shaddai is unknown; suggestions include “mountain” and “sufficient”. “Almighty” comes from early translations and fits the name’s use, of God’s power to give life and keep his promises. Naomi’s meaning does not depend on settling it.
verseByVerse.note: “Naomi” means “pleasant”; “Mara” means “bitter” (ESV notes). “The Almighty” is Shaddai.

verseByVerse.quote: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. And they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of barley harvest. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi comes home with Ruth the Moabite just as the barley harvest begins, and the chapter of emptying ends on a note of quiet hope.

So Naomi returned. A summary that turns the story towards hope.

Ruth the Moabite. A label that will recur through the book, keeping her outsider status before us so that her welcome lands with full force. She “returned” from Moab, though she had never been to Bethlehem: the return of faith, a soul’s homecoming to the people and the God of the covenant.

At the beginning of barley harvest. Barley ripened first, in spring, with wheat some weeks later (2:23). Just as Naomi declares herself empty, the fields are filling, and into them Ruth will go in chapter 2, to the field of a man named Boaz. Naomi sees only emptiness; God has already scheduled the harvest.

1.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Suffering. Naomi traces every loss directly to the hand of the LORD and the Almighty (vv. 13, 20–21). The book never suggests God is absent from the tragedy; he governs it. Naomi's error is to conclude that God's sovereign hand in her suffering means his heart is against her, and the narrator quietly corrects this by the closing note of harvest. What Romans 8:28 promises is already happening in this chapter, long before Naomi can see it: the God who empties is preparing to fill, working all things, even the deaths in Moab, toward a redemption that reaches to the manger of Bethlehem.

Hesed: Steadfast Covenant Love. Hesed is the word for God’s own covenant faithfulness, a love that stays loyal and gives more than duty strictly demands. Ruth's hesed toward Naomi (vv. 16–17) mirrors God's toward his people.

The Conversion of the Outsider. Ruth's "your God my God" is one of the great conversions of the Old Testament. A Moabite, from a people barred from the assembly (Deut 23:3), casts herself on the LORD by sheer grace, an early sign of the gospel reaching the nations.
1.examples:
Then: A widow without husband or sons was among the most vulnerable people in the ancient world, economically destitute, without legal standing or future. Naomi's despair was not exaggerated. Ruth's decision to follow her meant choosing that same poverty and uncertainty in a foreign land over the security of home.

Now: Naomi warns us against reading our circumstances too soon as God's final verdict. Ruth models the all-in commitment of faith, choosing loyal love over self-protection; in an age that prizes keeping our options open, her ‘where you go I will go’ shows us that following Christ is a binding, lifelong commitment. That loyalty is not summoned by willpower: it answers a God whose steadfast love came first, and it is the fruit his Spirit now grows in his people (Gal 5:22). If you are reading this freshly bereaved, or after years of hoping for a child who has not come, Naomi’s words are in Scripture so that you may say yours: God is not offended by an honest cry. And her conclusion that the LORD was against her was not the last word. The Son of David who came from this family took the real forsakenness on the cross (Mark 15:34), so that nothing, not even death, can separate God’s people from his love (Rom 8:31–39).

keyVerse.quote: For where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.
keyVerse.note: Ruth’s vow is the turning point of the chapter and the hinge of the whole book. In it a Moabite leaves her people and her gods and takes the LORD as her God, and everything that follows, from the gleaning field to the cradle of David, grows from this act of faith. It is also a small human likeness of the loyal love God shows his people in Christ.

1.reflection:
Naomi speaks honestly to God and about God in her grief (vv. 13, 20–21). What does her example teach about bringing bitterness and disappointment to God rather than hiding it? Where was she right, and where was she mistaken?

The family went to “sojourn” in Moab and instead “remained there” (vv. 1–2). Where are you tempted to settle gradually into a place, habit or compromise you never meant to stay in?

Orpah’s choice was reasonable; Ruth’s was costly (vv. 14–17). What did Ruth give up, and what did she gain? What would it look like for you to say “your God my God” when it costs something?

Ruth’s vow is a small picture of God binding himself to his people in Christ (Hebrews 13:5). How does knowing that God has not kept his options open with you give you courage to be faithful to others?

2.title: Under His Wings
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.<sup>2</sup>And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I shall find favor." And she said to her, "Go, my daughter."<sup>3</sup>So she set out and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech.<sup>4</sup>And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" And they answered, "The LORD bless you."<sup>5</sup>Then Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?"<sup>6</sup>And the servant who was in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman, who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.<sup>7</sup>She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest."<sup>8</sup>Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women.<sup>9</sup>Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn."<sup>10</sup>Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?"<sup>11</sup>But Boaz answered her, "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me, and how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before.<sup>12</sup>The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!"<sup>13</sup>Then she said, "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants."<sup>14</sup>And at mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed to her roasted grain. And she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over.<sup>15</sup>When she rose to glean, Boaz instructed his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.<sup>16</sup>And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her."<sup>17</sup>So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley.<sup>18</sup>And she took it up and went into the city. Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. She also brought out and gave her what food she had left over after being satisfied.<sup>19</sup>And her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? And where have you worked? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked and said, "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz."<sup>20</sup>And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours, one of our redeemers."<sup>21</sup>And Ruth the Moabite said, "Besides, he said to me, 'You shall keep close by my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'"<sup>22</sup>And Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, lest in another field you be assaulted."<sup>23</sup>So she kept close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
2.overview:
Where we are. Naomi and Ruth have come home to Bethlehem empty, just as the barley harvest begins (1:22). Chapter 2 moves out of grief into the open fields: the second of the book’s four scenes, provided for.

The message. God provides for those who take refuge under his wings, through ordinary work and generous people, often before they know it. Ruth goes out to glean, “happens” upon the field of a kinsman, and finds in Boaz a man whose kindness goes far beyond what the law required. Behind Boaz’s open hand is the open hand of God, whose kindness, Naomi now confesses, “has not forsaken the living or the dead” (v. 20).

Why it was said. In an age when the law was widely ignored (see the introduction), the first hearers are shown what Israel’s law looked like when someone actually lived it: a landowner who greets his workers in the LORD’s name, protects a vulnerable foreigner and feeds the poor with dignity. And they are shown that God’s hand is in what looks like chance.

How the chapter makes its case. The narrator tells us about Boaz before anyone in the story thinks of him, and then Ruth sets out to glean and “happened” to come to his field (vv. 1–3). Boaz arrives, notices her, and gives her protection, water, a place at his table and handfuls of grain left on purpose, blessing her by the God “under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (vv. 4–17). Ruth brings home an ephah of barley; Naomi hears the name, blesses the LORD for his kindness and calls Boaz “one of our redeemers”, and Ruth gleans with his workers until the harvests end (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God it reveals. Boaz is a kinsman with the right to redeem, who gives freely and beyond the law to a foreigner with no claim on him, and so foreshadows the Redeemer who became our kinsman (Hebrews 2:14–17). The wings under which Ruth takes refuge are the wings Jesus longed to spread over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37). And Ruth’s question, “Why have I found favor in your eyes… since I am a foreigner?” (v. 10), is the question every believer asks before the grace of God in Christ.

For us. There are no random fields in God’s world: thank him for the providences you did not arrange. And having been treated like Ruth, live like Boaz: generous beyond duty, protective of the vulnerable, leaving handfuls on purpose for others to find.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Ruth Goes Out to Glean
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Naomi or Ruth thinks of him, the narrator introduces Boaz: a worthy man and a kinsman of Elimelech (v. 1). Then the action begins with Ruth, not Naomi. She asks leave to glean behind anyone who will show her favour, using the right Israel’s law gave the poor and the foreigner, and Naomi lets her go (v. 2). She “happened” to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz (v. 3). The narrator tells it as luck, with a smile, because the reader already knows whose field it is: God is leading her to her redeemer without a word from heaven.
verseByVerse.theology: Providence is the book's engine, and it runs through people: Ruth's initiative, Naomi's consent, and a worthy man already standing in the right field.
verseByVerse.examples: Ruth does not sit passively waiting for provision; she goes out to hard, humble labor. Yet her diligence and God's providence are not in competition: she works, and God guides her steps. Believers labor faithfully in the ordinary, not to secure God's care but because they already rest in it, trusting that he governs the 'chances' that shape our lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's, a worthy man of the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator introduces Boaz to us before Naomi or Ruth thinks of him: a man of standing and a relative of Elimelech, the very man the story needs.

Now Naomi had a relative of her husband’s. The narrator steps aside to plant hope in the reader’s mind before the characters know of it. This is a known kinsman, “of the clan of Elimelech”, and a reader who knows that Israel’s law let a near relative redeem (rescue) a family in need at once senses possibility.

A worthy man. The phrase (gibbor hayil) is used of mighty warriors; here it means a man of wealth, standing and character. Ruth will be called the matching “worthy woman” (3:11). And his name is given at last: Boaz.

The reader knows first. We watch the providence unfold with eyes the characters do not yet have. God has put the answer in place before the need is felt, and the worthy man at the centre of it points beyond himself to the Redeemer who is strength and worth itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I shall find favor." And she said to her, "Go, my daughter." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth takes the initiative to go and glean, hoping for kindness she has no right to expect, and Naomi lets her go.

Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi. The outsider’s label again, so that the grace shown to her lands with full force. And it is Ruth, not Naomi, who acts; Naomi is still sunk in grief.

Let me go to the field and glean. Israel’s law told landowners not to reap the edges of their fields or pick up what was dropped, but to leave it for the poor, the widow and the sojourner (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 24:19–22). Gleaners gathered by hand, stalk by stalk. It was honest but humbling work, and not without danger for a foreign woman (v. 9).

In whose sight I shall find favor. Favour (hen) is the language of grace, undeserved kindness. Ruth knows she has no claim; she can only hope to find grace. She does not presume; she works and trusts. Naomi’s “Go, my daughter” is the first warm word she has spoken since her lament.

Is gleaning a model for helping the poor? The law gave the poor work, not a handout: they gathered for themselves what landowners left. As a law of the land it ended with Old Testament Israel as a nation under God’s direct rule, but its principles remain: provide for the poor with dignity, and leave room for them to work (Ephesians 4:28; 2 Thessalonians 3:10).
verseByVerse.note: Gleaners gathered by hand, stalk by stalk, which is why a full ephah in one day (v. 17) is remarkable.

verseByVerse.quote: So she set out and went and gleaned in the field after the reapers, and she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was of the clan of Elimelech. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth “happens” upon the field of Boaz: the narrator tells the most plainly God-arranged event in the story in the language of chance, and smiles as he does it.

She happened to come. Literally, “her chance chanced upon” the part of the field belonging to Boaz. We have just been told that he is Elimelech’s kinsman, and the narrator repeats it (“who was of the clan of Elimelech”) so that we cannot miss it: out of all the fields around Bethlehem, she “just happens” to glean in his.

No such thing as chance. The event most plainly arranged by God is told in the language of accident, to teach that in his world there is no such thing as chance. His hand is no less present in the ordinary than in the miracle, and he most often works through unremarked coincidences. Ruth thinks she is choosing a field; God is leading her to her redeemer.

Luck, or a hand? Most modern people live with two stories at once. Officially the universe is an accident and our lives are products of chance. In practice we cannot stop talking as if things were meant: the job that came at just the right time, the person we happened to sit next to. The French biologist Jacques Monod argued that we are here by pure chance, in a universe indifferent to our hopes. Few manage to live that way; we keep hearing a tune. The narrator of Ruth plays with exactly that tension. He uses the language of luck while showing us the hand, because the God of Israel rarely signs his work at the time. That is humbling, because it means we do not run our lives, and freeing, because it means our lives are not running loose. It reaches its height at the event that looked most like a tragic accident of all: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). If God was at work there, he is not absent from your field.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In one day Boaz shows Ruth a kindness that runs far beyond the law. He arrives with a blessing for his reapers and asks who the stranger is (vv. 4–7). He tells her to stay in his field, close to his young women, safe from his men, and to drink from his water (vv. 8–9). When she falls on her face in wonder, he explains that he has heard of her loyalty to Naomi, and prays that the LORD, under whose wings she has taken refuge, will reward her (vv. 10–13). He feeds her at his table, has his men drop extra grain for her, and she goes home with an ephah of barley (vv. 14–17).
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz embodies grace that goes beyond law (v. 16), and his blessing in v. 12 gives one of Scripture's tenderest images of God as a sheltering refuge.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models faith that saturates daily work. His first words to his laborers are a benediction; he treats a destitute foreign woman with dignity, generosity and protection. Piety is not confined to the temple but overflows into the field and the treatment of the vulnerable. God's care for the poor usually arrives through someone's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. And he said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you!" And they answered, "The LORD bless you." Then Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose young woman is this?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz arrives at just the right moment, a man whose faith shows in how he greets his workers, and at once he notices the stranger.

And behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem. “Behold” invites us to share the surprise: the providence that brought Ruth to the field now brings its owner.

The LORD be with you! His first words are a blessing on his workers, and they answer in kind. In the days when “everyone did what was right in his own eyes”, here is a man whose faith flows into his dealings with his labourers, where godliness is often hardest to sustain.

Whose young woman is this? A woman belonged to a household, so this is the natural question: whose family is she from? It opens the door to everything that follows: the redeemer has caught sight of the woman he will redeem.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant who was in charge of the reapers answered, "She is the young Moabite woman, who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab. She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now, except for a short rest." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foreman’s report shows Ruth’s humility and her hard work: she asked permission, took the lowest place and has worked since dawn.

She is the young Moabite woman. He knows her by her origin and by her link with Naomi; her story has gone round the town (v. 11).

Please let me glean. She asked permission, though the law gave her the right, and gleaned “after the reapers”, in the lowest place. She has worked from early morning with only a short rest. The narrator builds our admiration for her before Boaz’s generosity descends.

Faith that labours. Ruth’s hard work does not earn the grace that is coming, but it is where that grace finds her. Faith trusts God and gets up early.

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 7 is among the hardest Hebrew in the book; word for word it runs something like “this her sitting in the house a little”. It may mean she rested briefly in a field shelter, or hardly rested at all. Some think her request to gather “among the sheaves” was for more than a gleaner’s usual right, so that she had been waiting for the owner’s permission; that would explain why Boaz later grants exactly that (v. 15). The general sense, that she has been humble and diligent, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to Ruth, "Now, listen, my daughter, do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but keep close to my young women. Let your eyes be on the field that they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? And when you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz takes Ruth under his protection: she is to stay in his field, close to his women and safe from his men, and drink from his water.

Now, listen, my daughter. Tender and protective. Boaz is older (3:10) and speaks as a guardian, putting the foreigner at ease.

Keep close to my young women. She is to stay in his field rather than wander where she might be exposed, and glean alongside his women under his household’s protection.

Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? Protection from harassment or assault for a young foreign widow who was dangerously vulnerable (v. 22). And she may drink what his young men have drawn: the foreigner is served, where she might have expected to serve.

The wings begin to spread. Boaz’s care pictures the way Christ shelters his own: he does not merely let the vulnerable come near; he guards them. Before any thought of marriage Boaz is already acting as a kind of redeemer, and the wings he will pray for in verse 12 are beginning to spread over Ruth.

For us. A church, a workplace or a home that bears Christ’s name should be a place where the vulnerable are safe, and those in charge should make it so in advance, as Boaz did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she fell on her face, bowing to the ground, and said to him, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth falls on her face, astonished that a man like Boaz should notice a foreigner with no claim on him; her question is the wonder of every soul that meets grace.

She fell on her face, bowing to the ground. A posture of deep humility and gratitude.

Why have I found favor in your eyes? Favour is again hen, unmerited kindness, and “foreigner” (nokriyah) stresses that she has no claim at all: a Moabite, from a people barred from the assembly.

That you should take notice of me, since I am a foreigner. A wordplay runs through the Hebrew: “take notice” (nakar) and “foreigner” (nokriyah) sound alike, as if she said, “Why have you recognised me, the one nobody recognises?” The very thing that should have made her invisible has become the occasion for grace.

The wonder of grace. Her question is the believer’s before God: why should I, who have no right, be shown such kindness? God notices those who have no claim, the people once “strangers to the covenants of promise” and now “brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:12–13), and the believer never gets over the question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Boaz answered her, "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me, and how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz has heard everything Ruth has done for Naomi; like Abraham, she left her land and kindred for a people she did not know.

Fully told to me. Her reputation has gone before her: her loyalty to Naomi since her husband’s death, and her leaving father, mother and native land.

You left your father and mother and your native land. An echo of God’s call to Abraham to leave “your country and your kindred and your father’s house” (Genesis 12:1). Ruth has made an Abraham-like journey of faith; she is a daughter of Abraham by faith, not by blood, exactly what Paul would teach: “it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham” (Galatians 3:7).

Not earned but given. We must not mistake the order. Ruth’s loyalty does not earn the redemption to come; it is the fruit of the faith that has already taken hold of her. Boaz commends what grace has produced.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz prays that the LORD will fully reward Ruth, for she has come to shelter under his wings like a chick under a mother bird; and Boaz himself will become the answer to his prayer.

The LORD repay you. A blessing, not wages: he asks God to give her “a full reward”.

Under whose wings. The word (kanaf) is the wing of a bird, and it pictures the God of Israel as a mother bird sheltering her young. Ruth has come not merely to Bethlehem but to refuge under the LORD’s wings. This is the heart of saving faith: fleeing to God as one’s shelter.

Refuge through Scripture. The image runs like a golden thread through the Bible: “in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge” (Psalm 57:1); “he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4). It reaches its most moving form on the lips of Jesus weeping over Jerusalem: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The God under whose wings Ruth sheltered came in person, and spread his arms on a cross.

Boaz answers his own prayer. In 3:9 Ruth will ask him to spread his own “wings” (the same word, there the corner of his garment) over her. He prays a prayer God will answer through him. That is often how God answers our prayers for others: by sending the one who prayed.
verseByVerse.note: “Wings” can also mean the corners of a garment (ESV note at 3:9), the same word Ruth uses to Boaz.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she said, "I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth thanks Boaz for comforting her with kind words, though she has no standing even as one of his servants.

I have found favor in your eyes, my lord. The grace she wondered at in verse 10 she now receives.

You have comforted me and spoken kindly. Literally, “spoken to the heart”, the idiom of Isaiah’s “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:2). Comfort at last for a woman who came in sorrow: his words have done what no grain could.

Though I am not one of your servants. She has no place in his household, which makes his kindness the more astonishing. This is the posture of the redeemed: neither grovelling nor presuming, receiving with open hands what she has not earned. It is the comfort of the gospel in miniature: to be spoken to tenderly by one who had every right to ignore us.

verseByVerse.quote: And at mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come here and eat some bread and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sat beside the reapers, and he passed to her roasted grain. And she ate until she was satisfied, and she had some left over. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz brings Ruth to his table and serves her with his own hand, and she eats until she is satisfied, with food to spare.

Come here and eat some bread. To share a meal was to extend belonging. The foreign gleaner sits with his reapers, and the master passes her roasted grain himself. The bread was dipped in “wine”, probably a sour wine that refreshed workers in the heat.

She ate until she was satisfied. Fullness, more than enough, for a woman from a household marked by famine and emptiness. And she had some left over, which she will carry home (v. 18).

Served by the lord of the harvest. Many Christians have heard a gospel echo here: a foreigner welcomed to a table she had no right to, served by the master himself, and satisfied. It is a foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), where people from every nation are fed by the Lord who, Jesus said, “will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them” (Luke 12:37).

verseByVerse.quote: When she rose to glean, Boaz instructed his young men, saying, "Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her. And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean, and do not rebuke her." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of Ruth’s hearing, Boaz tells his men to let her glean among the sheaves and to drop extra grain for her on purpose: grace beyond the law, given in secret.

Let her glean even among the sheaves. The law let the poor gather from the edges and what was dropped (Leviticus 19:9–10). Among the sheaves the harvest itself was being gathered, and gleaners were normally kept away. Boaz lets her in, and has his men pull stalks from the bundles and leave them for her. Twice he tells them not to shame her.

Beyond the law’s floor. The law set a floor for provision; Boaz’s kindness has no ceiling, and he gives in secret, so that she experiences it simply as the bounty of the field. The older English versions caught the phrase beautifully: “handfuls of purpose” (Ruth 2:16, KJV).

Handfuls on purpose. That is how the grace of God works. He does not deal with us by the strict requirements of the law; he orders our circumstances so that grace overflows where we least expect it. Behind the undeserved kindnesses that meet us is a Redeemer who has quietly arranged our lives to bless us beyond all merit.

For us. Give like Boaz, so that the one who receives keeps her dignity: “when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3).

verseByVerse.quote: So she gleaned in the field until evening. Then she beat out what she had gleaned, and it was about an ephah of barley. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth works until evening and beats out about an ephah of barley, far more than any gleaner could expect: Boaz’s hidden generosity, weighed out.

She beat out what she had gleaned. She threshed it by hand with a stick, to separate the grain from the stalks.

About an ephah of barley. An ephah was about three-fifths of a bushel, perhaps thirteen kilograms (thirty pounds) of grain, enough to feed two women for weeks. For a gleaner, a day’s yield like that was extraordinary: it is Boaz’s handfuls on purpose, now in the basket.

From empty to full. The contrast with chapter 1 is deliberate. The God who emptied Naomi (1:21) is beginning to fill her again, through Boaz’s kindness and a day’s honest work. God often pours out his most lavish gifts through the most ordinary channels.
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note), far more than a gleaner could expect.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At home the kindness of Boaz becomes, for Naomi, the kindness of the LORD. Ruth shows her the grain and the food she saved from her meal (v. 18). Naomi asks where she worked, blesses the man before she knows his name, and when she hears it is Boaz she blesses the LORD, “whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead”, and explains that he is one of their redeemers (vv. 19–20). The bitter woman of chapter 1 begins to hope. Ruth reports the invitation to stay for the whole harvest; Naomi urges her to keep with his women for safety; and Ruth gleans through the barley and wheat harvests, living with her mother-in-law (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The key word emerges: go'el, kinsman-redeemer. Naomi recognizes Boaz as 'one of our redeemers' (v. 20), and for the first time since her lament she calls on the LORD to bless, declaring that his hesed has not forsaken the living or the dead. The hidden providence of chapter 1 is becoming visible.
verseByVerse.examples: Bitterness rarely yields to argument. It often begins to thaw when someone's practical kindness becomes evidence of God's, as a basket of barley did for Naomi.

verseByVerse.quote: And she took it up and went into the city. Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. She also brought out and gave her what food she had left over after being satisfied. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth carries the grain home and gives Naomi the food she saved from her meal: grace received becomes grace shared.

Her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. Such a quantity from a single day could only mean that something remarkable had happened in the field.

What food she had left over. Ruth did not keep the surplus from Boaz’s table; she brought it home (v. 14). The destitute foreigner is feeding the Israelite widow, and Naomi, who called herself “empty”, sees fullness carried through her door by the daughter-in-law she tried to send away.

Grace overflows. Grace received overflows in grace given; the one who has been filled cannot help but share. Ruth’s hesed towards Naomi goes on: she works all day, saves part of her meal, and brings it home.

verseByVerse.quote: And her mother-in-law said to her, "Where did you glean today? And where have you worked? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she told her mother-in-law with whom she had worked and said, "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi eagerly asks where Ruth gleaned and blesses the man before she knows his name; then Ruth tells her: Boaz.

Where did you glean today? The questions tumble out; such a harvest could only come from extraordinary kindness.

Blessed be the man who took notice of you. “Took notice” (nakar) is Ruth’s word in verse 10. Naomi blesses the man before she knows who he is.

The man’s name with whom I worked today is Boaz. The narrator saves the name for the very end, and it lands with its full weight. The reader has known since verse 1. Now Naomi will see what Ruth could not: the generous stranger is a kinsman placed by God, and hope, long dead in her, is about to draw breath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, "May he be blessed by the LORD, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" Naomi also said to her, "The man is a close relative of ours, one of our redeemers." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing the name, Naomi blesses the LORD, whose loyal love has not abandoned her family, and recognises Boaz as one of their redeemers: the turning point of her soul.

May he be blessed by the LORD. In 1:20–21 she said the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her; now she blesses God for his kindness, his hesed, towards “the living”, herself and Ruth, and “the dead”, Elimelech and her sons, whose line may yet be saved.

One of our redeemers. The pivotal word of the book: go’el. Under Israel’s law the redeemer was a near relative with the right and duty to rescue family members in distress: to buy back land sold in poverty (Leviticus 25:25), to redeem a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–49), and to avenge a murdered kinsman (Numbers 35:19). Naomi sees at once what it might mean.

He became our near kinsman. The redeemer is a pattern that Christ fulfils. He became our kinsman by taking our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14–17), so that “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and he has the right, the resources and the will to redeem his people.

Uncertain wording. In “whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead”, the Hebrew could refer to the LORD or to Boaz. Most take it of the LORD, as in the similar blessing of Genesis 24:27, “Blessed be the LORD… who has not forsaken his steadfast love”. If it means Boaz, the point is the same: through Boaz the LORD’s kindness has reached them.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word is go'el. Boaz is "one of" Naomi's redeemers, and there is a nearer one (3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And Ruth the Moabite said, "Besides, he said to me, 'You shall keep close by my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth adds that Boaz has invited her to stay with his workers until the whole harvest is over: provision not for a day but for a season.

And Ruth the Moabite said. Still “the Moabite”, even as redemption dawns.

Until they have finished all my harvest. Not one day’s mercy but security for the barley and wheat harvests, weeks of provision. The kindnesses have piled up: protection, water, a meal, extra grain, and now a welcome for the whole season. Ruth simply rejoices in the security; Naomi sees where it may lead.

Keep close by my young men. In verse 8 Boaz had said “my young women”. Ruth reports it more loosely, and Naomi gently steers her back to the women in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, lest in another field you be assaulted." So she kept close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lived with her mother-in-law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi, alert now for Ruth’s good, urges her to stay with Boaz’s women for safety, and Ruth gleans there through both harvests, still living with her mother-in-law.

Lest in another field you be assaulted. The woman once passive in grief now plans for Ruth’s protection; she knows how real the danger was for a foreign widow.

Until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. About seven weeks, from the barley in spring to the wheat in early summer, the span later marked by the Feast of Weeks (Deuteronomy 16:9–10), the festival at which Jewish custom reads this book (see the introduction).

And she lived with her mother-in-law. Ruth did not drift away once provision was secured; she kept her vow.

Setting the stage. Daily bread is secured and the redeemer identified. Chapter 3 turns to the deeper question, from gleaning to redemption, from bread for a season to rest for a lifetime.
verseByVerse.note: Barley and wheat harvests together ran about seven weeks, from Passover to Pentecost.

2.theology:
The Hidden Providence of God. Chapter 2 shows how God's sovereignty ordinarily operates: not chiefly through spectacular miracle but through 'coincidence' and the faithful obedience of ordinary people (v. 3). What Ruth experiences as chance is the orchestration of a sovereign Lord who has already positioned her redeemer (v. 1).

Grace Beyond Law. The gleaning laws set a floor of provision for the poor; Boaz has grain pulled from the bundles and left for her on purpose (v. 16). God does not deal with his people according to strict legal measure but pours out abundance we could never earn.

The Refuge of God's Wings. Boaz's blessing in v. 12 presents God as a sheltering mother bird, and this is the picture of saving faith: fleeing to God for refuge. The image culminates on the lips of Jesus, who longed to gather Jerusalem 'as a hen gathers her brood under her wings' (Matt 23:37).
2.examples:
Then: Gleaning was Israel's social safety net for the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner, a divinely mandated provision that required landowners to leave the edges of their fields, and whatever the reapers dropped, for the destitute. Boaz's protection of Ruth, his water and food, and his extra grain all went far beyond what the law required, modeling the heart of God toward the marginalized.

Now: Begin where Ruth began, with her wonder: 'Why have I found favor in your eyes?' Grace found us when we had no claim, and Christ our Redeemer has given us far more than any law required. Out of that, Boaz shows us faith filling ordinary work and business. Godliness is most credible where it is hardest: in the marketplace, and in our treatment of those who can do nothing for us. The Spirit who has made us God's own makes us his 'handfuls on purpose' in the fields of a hurting world, for the hidden providence of God so often reaches the vulnerable through the open hands of his people.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD repay you for what you have done, and a full reward be given you by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!
keyVerse.note: Boaz’s blessing names what Ruth has done in coming to Israel: she has taken refuge under the wings of its God. It is the picture of saving faith that runs through the Psalms to Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem. And it sets up the turn of the book, for in 3:9 Ruth will ask Boaz to spread his own “wings” over her, and he will become the answer to his own prayer.

2.reflection:
The narrator says Ruth “happened” to come to Boaz’s field (v. 3), while showing us God’s hand. Can you look back on “coincidences” in your own life that you now see as God’s providence? How does that change the way you face what you cannot yet see?

Boaz greets his workers in the LORD’s name, protects a vulnerable woman and gives beyond what the law required, in secret (vv. 4, 8–9, 15–16). What would it look like to bring that kind of godliness into your work, your home or your church?

Ruth asks, “Why have I found favor in your eyes… since I am a foreigner?” (v. 10). How is her wonder like the wonder of being accepted by God in Christ? Has that wonder grown dim for you?

Naomi moves from “the LORD has brought me back empty” (1:21) to blessing the LORD for his unfailing kindness (v. 20). What brought about the change? Who in your life might need you to be the means by which they see God’s kindness again?

3.title: The Bold Request
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?<sup>2</sup>Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor.<sup>3</sup>Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak and go down to the threshing floor, but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.<sup>4</sup>But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do."<sup>5</sup>And she replied, "All that you say I will do."<sup>6</sup>So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her.<sup>7</sup>And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down.<sup>8</sup>At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet!<sup>9</sup>He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich.<sup>11</sup>And now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman.<sup>12</sup>And now it is true that I am a redeemer. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I.<sup>13</sup>Remain tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until the morning."<sup>14</sup>So she lay at his feet until the morning, but arose before one could recognize another. And he said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city.<sup>16</sup>And when she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did you fare, my daughter?" Then she told her all that the man had done for her,<sup>17</sup>saying, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said to me, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'"<sup>18</sup>She replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest but will settle the matter today."
3.overview:
Where we are. The barley and wheat harvests are over (2:23). Ruth has had bread for a season, but she and Naomi still have no future. This is the third of the book’s four scenes: the appeal to the redeemer.

The message. Redemption is asked for, and promised. Ruth comes by night to the man who has the right to redeem and asks him to spread his wings over her, not because she is worthy but because he is a redeemer. Boaz answers with blessing, with an oath, and with a gift that means she will not go home empty. Faith comes boldly to the redeemer on the ground of who he is, and finds him both more willing than it dared hope and scrupulously just.

Why it was said. Israel knew how easily a harvest night at the threshing floor could mean sin (Hosea 9:1). The first hearers, under the house of David (see the introduction), are shown that the founders of their royal line acted with purity and honour where everything could have gone wrong, and that the law’s provision for the helpless was meant to be honoured, not dodged.

How the chapter makes its case. Naomi seeks “rest” for Ruth and lays out a bold plan: wash, anoint yourself, go down to the threshing floor, uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do (vv. 1–5).
