At midnight Boaz wakes to find her there; she asks him to spread his wings over her, “for you are a redeemer”; he blesses her as a worthy woman and swears to redeem her if the nearer redeemer will not (vv. 6–13). Before dawn he sends her home unseen with six measures of barley for Naomi, and Naomi tells her to wait, for “the man will not rest” (vv. 14–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. Ruth approaches the kinsman-redeemer on the ground of his office, and he answers with a promise sealed by oath and a pledge of what he will do. So sinners come to Christ: not “I am worthy” but “you are the Redeemer”, and he has bound himself with an oath to receive them (Hebrews 6:17–18). And the redeemer who will not rest until the matter is settled points to the one who did not rest until he could say, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

For us. Come to Christ boldly, on the ground of who he is, and then wait in peace while he finishes what he has begun. And in a world where opportunity for sin is everywhere and unseen, guard the honour of others as Boaz guarded Ruth’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the harvest over, Naomi sets out to secure for Ruth not bread for a season but rest for a lifetime. Her plan is bold and full of risk. Ruth is to wash, anoint herself and put on her cloak, go down by night to the threshing floor where Boaz, their kinsman, is winnowing, and wait until he has eaten and lain down; then she is to uncover his feet and lie there, and he will tell her what to do (vv. 1–4). In that culture it was a silent appeal to him to act as redeemer. Ruth trusts Naomi completely: “All that you say I will do” (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The plan, culturally bold and morally precarious, aims to invoke the law of the kinsman-redeemer to secure Ruth's future and preserve Elimelech's line. Naomi's change from despairing widow to active matchmaker shows faith beginning to hope and act again.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi seeks not merely Ruth's survival but her flourishing, not just bread but a home. Genuine love looks beyond immediate needs to lasting good. Yet the plan carries real risk, reminding us that faithful people act within imperfect circumstances, planning wisely while the result rests in God's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi her mother-in-law said to her, "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you, that it may be well with you?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now that the harvest is over, Naomi sets out to find Ruth a lasting home: not bread for a season but rest for a lifetime.

Should I not seek rest for you? Naomi takes the initiative, a striking change from the grief-stricken woman of chapter 1. “Rest” means a settled home, security and belonging. It is what she prayed for in 1:9, “that you may find rest, each of you in the house of her husband”, and now she sets out to become the means by which her own prayer is answered. She has come a long way from “call me Mara”.

That it may be well with you. That is what real love seeks: not only relief for today but lasting good.

Rest in God. The rest Naomi seeks for Ruth foreshadows the rest the gospel gives, the secure belonging that comes through redemption: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). As Augustine famously prayed, our hearts are restless until they find their rest in God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See, he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak and go down to the threshing floor, but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what to do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi’s plan is bold: Ruth is to make herself ready, go to the threshing floor at night and lie at Boaz’s feet, a silent request that he take up his part as redeemer.

Is not Boaz our relative? The plan rests on his kinship: he is one of their redeemers (2:20).

He is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor. The threshing floor was a hard, open space where the threshed grain was tossed into the evening breeze so that the chaff blew away. At harvest, owners often slept beside the heaps to guard them.

Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your cloak. Preparations for an important meeting. Going without oil was a sign of mourning (2 Samuel 14:2), so Ruth may be putting off the ways of widowhood and presenting herself as a woman ready to marry.

Uncover his feet and lie down. Read with her words in verse 9, the gesture is a silent request: she places herself at his feet, under his protection, and leaves the decision to him. “He will tell you what to do”: Naomi is staking everything on the integrity of a worthy man and the providence of God.

What it does not mean. This is not a pattern for engineering a romance by night. The means belonged to that custom and that moment; what abides is bold faith joined to purity.

Was “uncover his feet” sexual? Some read it as a euphemism or a seduction, and the scene does use words that can carry double meanings (“lie down”, “know”), which raise the tension. But the text says feet, Boaz calls her a worthy woman (v. 11), and he sends her home before anyone sees her, protecting her name. It was a bold, unusual request for marriage, made in a way that left the decision to him.

Uncertain wording. The word for “feet” here (margelot) is rare; it seems to mean “the place of the feet”, and elsewhere it is used of legs (Daniel 10:6). The likely meaning is that she uncovered his feet or legs to the night air, so that he would wake and find her.

verseByVerse.quote: And she replied, "All that you say I will do." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth agrees at once to do all that Naomi says, trusting her mother-in-law and the God under whose wings she has taken refuge.

All that you say I will do. No hesitation and no calculation of the risk. The same loyalty that bound her to Naomi at the crossroads now governs her willingness to follow this bold plan.

Quiet courage. A foreign widow whose reputation is all she has agrees to a plan that could be disastrously misunderstood. This is the obedience of faith: stepping into a risky and unclear place, trusting the guidance she has been given and the God who governs the outcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the dark at the threshing floor, Ruth asks the redeemer to redeem her, and Boaz answers with honour. She does as Naomi said and lies at his feet (vv. 6–7). At midnight Boaz wakes and finds her (v. 8). She names herself his servant and asks him to spread his wings over her, for he is a redeemer (v. 9). He blesses her, calls her request a greater kindness than all she has done, and promises to do all she asks, for the whole town knows her as a worthy woman (vv. 10–11). But a nearer redeemer has the first right, so Boaz swears by the LORD to redeem her if that man will not (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz is willing, but he will not cut corners: he honours the nearer kinsman's prior claim, so that redemption proceeds in righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Character is tested where nobody is watching. Boaz had every opportunity in the dark and used none of it; he protected a vulnerable woman's honor and acted justly.

verseByVerse.quote: So she went down to the threshing floor and did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her. And when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth does as she was told: when Boaz has eaten and lain down by the grain heap, she comes quietly, uncovers his feet and lies down.

She went down to the threshing floor. She “did just as her mother-in-law had commanded her”, with one difference to come: instead of waiting for Boaz to tell her what to do, she will speak first (v. 9).

His heart was merry. The good cheer of a harvest meal. The narrator gives no hint that he was drunk and guards his dignity. He lies down “at the end of the heap of grain”, guarding the harvest through the night.

She came softly. Every word is charged with risk; a single misunderstanding could ruin Ruth’s name and Naomi’s hopes. Ruth has done the bold thing faith required; now she lies in the dark and waits, her future hanging on what the worthy man will do when he wakes.

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
At midnight Boaz wakes with a start to find a woman lying at his feet, and the whole story hangs on what this man will do in the dark.

At midnight the man was startled and turned over. The deepest dark of the night. The word suggests a sudden shudder, perhaps at the cold on his feet. “Behold” lets us see through his astonished eyes: a woman lies at his feet, and he does not know who she is or why she is there.

The hinge of the chapter. How will a worthy man respond when no one is watching and he could do anything? What a man does in the dark shows who he is. The darkness of the threshing floor will make Ruth’s faith and Boaz’s righteousness shine the brighter.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Who are you?" And she answered, "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth names herself and asks Boaz to spread his wings over her, that is, to marry and protect her, because he is a redeemer.

I am Ruth, your servant. She gives her name and presumes on no status. Her word for “servant” is not the one she used in 2:13; it is the word for a maidservant who could become a wife.

Spread your wings over your servant. The very word (kanaf) of Boaz’s prayer in 2:12, that she would be rewarded by the LORD “under whose wings you have come to take refuge”. Ruth turns his prayer back on him: you prayed that I would find refuge under God’s wings; now spread your wing over me. To spread the corner of one’s garment over a woman was an idiom for marriage and protection; God uses it of his covenant with Israel: “I spread the corner of my garment over you” (Ezekiel 16:8). See Weddings and Betrothal.

For you are a redeemer. She grounds her appeal not in her worthiness but in his role: you are a redeemer, so redeem me. And she asks for more than the law strictly required of him: a marriage that would raise up a family for the dead (4:5, 10).

How the soul comes to Christ. This is how we come to Christ: not “I am worthy”, but “you are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me”. He made himself our kinsman for this very purpose, and he has promised, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: “Spread your wings” uses the word for corners of a garment (ESV note): a request for marriage and protection.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. You have made this last kindness greater than the first in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz blesses Ruth and calls her request a greater act of loyal love than all she has done for Naomi, for she has chosen him, for the family’s sake, over younger men.

May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter. No offence, no exploitation, no suspicion: his first instinct is to call down God’s blessing on her.

This last kindness greater than the first. “Kindness” is again hesed. The first was her loyalty to Naomi; the last and greater is that she has sought marriage with an older kinsman, which would carry on her dead husband’s line and provide for Naomi, rather than going after young men, poor or rich. She has put the family above her own wishes.

A noble response. A lesser man might have been flattered or taken advantage. Boaz is humbled and grateful, and thinks only of her honour and welfare. A midnight meeting that could have become a scandal becomes a pledge of honour and blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, my daughter, do not fear. I will do for you all that you ask, for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman. And now it is true that I am a redeemer. Yet there is a redeemer nearer than I. Remain tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, good; let him do it. But if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until the morning." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz promises to do all that Ruth asks, for she is known as a worthy woman; but a nearer redeemer has the first right, and Boaz swears that if he will not act, he will.

Do not fear. He calms her, and “I will do for you all that you ask” commits him to her cause.

You are a worthy woman. The phrase (eshet hayil) is the counterpart of the “worthy man” (gibbor hayil) of 2:1, and it is the phrase that crowns Proverbs, “An excellent wife” (Proverbs 31:10). The whole town has seen her character; her nationality and her poverty do not count against it. The worthy man and the worthy woman belong together.

There is a redeemer nearer than I. Boaz will not take the role by going round the proper order, even at the risk of losing her. Yet he seals his commitment with an oath: “as the LORD lives, I will redeem you.” And he keeps her safe until morning rather than send her through the dark streets alone.

The right, but not the willingness. As chapter 4 will show, the nearer redeemer has the right but not the willingness. Some Christians have seen in him a picture of the law, which has a prior claim on us but cannot redeem (see the note on 4:6). Christ has both the right and the will, and God has bound his promise with an oath, so that we may have “strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us” (Hebrews 6:18).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz protects Ruth’s name and sends her home with a pledge, and Naomi tells her to wait. Ruth leaves before dawn, before anyone can recognise her, so that no gossip can spoil what Boaz intends (v. 14). He fills her cloak with six measures of barley, a generous gift and a sign of his intent (v. 15). At home she tells Naomi everything and repeats his words: she must not go back empty-handed to her mother-in-law (vv. 16–17). Naomi answers with settled confidence: wait, for the man will not rest until he has settled the matter today (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The barley is provision and promise together, a pledge from the redeemer of what he will do.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz's care in sending Ruth away before dawn models the care genuine love takes for the honor of the beloved, and his gift shows commitment expressed in tangible provision.

verseByVerse.quote: So she lay at his feet until the morning, but arose before one could recognize another. And he said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth stays until just before dawn and leaves unrecognised, and Boaz protects her good name.

She lay at his feet until the morning. In complete propriety. She rises in the grey before dawn, “before one could recognize another”.

Let it not be known. Not the secrecy of guilt but the wisdom of honour. Boaz knows how easily the night could be misread, and gossip about it could also cloud the public redemption he intends at the city gate. He guards her name as carefully as his own.

For us. Love protects other people’s reputations, and avoids even what could be misread when someone else would pay the price (Romans 14:16).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz fills Ruth’s cloak with six measures of barley, a generous gift and a pledge of his intent.

Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out. A shawl or cloak that could be held out as a sack. He measured the grain into it and lifted the load onto her.

A pledge. The gift means that Ruth will not go home empty-handed (v. 17), and it says without words that he means what he has sworn: a down payment on the redemption to come. The woman who declared herself empty is receiving, measure by measure, the filling of grace.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew says only “six of barley”; the unit is not named. It cannot have been six ephahs, far too heavy to carry, so most think of a smaller measure, perhaps six scoopfuls. It was clearly generous. The text does not say why six, and guessing at the number distracts from what the gesture plainly is.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she came to her mother-in-law, she said, "How did you fare, my daughter?" Then she told her all that the man had done for her, saying, "These six measures of barley he gave to me, for he said to me, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ruth tells Naomi everything and shows her the barley, with Boaz’s words: “You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.”

How did you fare, my daughter? Literally, “Who are you, my daughter?”, probably meaning, “How do things stand with you now?”

You must not go back empty-handed. These words appear only in Ruth’s report, and “empty-handed” is the word Naomi used in 1:21: “the LORD has brought me back empty.” Boaz’s care reaches Naomi too. The God who emptied her is now, through his chosen redeemer, beginning to fill her.

verseByVerse.quote: She replied, "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out, for the man will not rest but will settle the matter today." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi tells Ruth to wait, confident that Boaz will not rest until he has settled the matter that very day.

Wait, my daughter. Literally “sit”. Having done all that faith required, Ruth can now only rest in the redeemer’s faithfulness.

The man will not rest. Naomi knows his integrity; having pledged himself, he will see it through that very day. And there is a gentle irony: Naomi sought rest for Ruth (v. 1), and Ruth can sit still precisely because Boaz will not.

He will bring it to completion. The believer’s rest rests on the Redeemer’s commitment to finish what he has begun: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Christ did not rest until he could say, “It is finished” (John 19:30), and he will not rest until his people are fully and finally his. The bride waits in peace, for everything now depends on the faithfulness of the one who has pledged to redeem her.

3.theology:
The Willing Redeemer. Ruth appeals to Boaz not on the basis of her worth but of his identity: 'you are a redeemer' (v. 9). Boaz responds with blessing, honor and an unconditional pledge sealed by oath (vv. 10–13). This willingness is the heart of what the book shows us about Christ. A redeemer must have the right, the resources and the willingness to redeem. Boaz did not have to redeem Ruth; he chose to, out of love. So Christ came willingly, and it is his willingness the gospel celebrates: he loved us and gave himself for us (Gal 2:20).

Spread Your Wings: The Prayer Answered Through the Pray-er. Ruth's request (v. 9) deliberately echoes Boaz's own prayer in 2:12, and asks him to become the human means by which God answers it. God often answers our prayers for others by making us the instrument of the very blessing we requested. God shelters people under his wings through the care his obedient people give, and supremely through Christ, who gathers his own to himself.

The Posture of Saving Faith. Ruth comes in lowliness ('your servant'), in boldness ('spread your wings over me'), and in confident appeal to his role ('you are a redeemer'). This is the posture of the soul coming to Christ: not pleading our own merit but appealing to who he is, the Savior. We do not say to Christ, 'I am worthy'; we say, 'You are the Redeemer; cover me.'
3.examples:
Then: The customs of the kinsman-redeemer and levirate marriage (Lev 25:25; Deut 25:5–10) lie behind Ruth’s bold approach. Her request that Boaz spread his garment over her was a recognized idiom for marriage and protection, and both of them acted with complete integrity in a scene that could easily have caused scandal.

Now: Ruth teaches us how to come to our Redeemer: not with pride in our achievements but with the bold humility that says, 'You are the Redeemer; spread your wings over me.' We approach Christ empty-handed, appealing not to our worth but to his role and his willingness. Boaz models a love that guards the honor of the beloved, acts in righteousness rather than seizing advantage, and gives tangible pledges of commitment. And Naomi's counsel to 'wait' teaches the restful patience of faith: having done all, we trust the One who 'will not rest but will settle the matter today,' confident that he who began a good work will complete it. The chapter is not a template for night-time visits: its custom belonged to its world. What carries over is the integrity on both sides, Ruth’s bold honesty and the way Boaz guards her name.

keyVerse.quote: I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant, for you are a redeemer.
keyVerse.note: Ruth’s request is the turning point of the book. She takes the words of Boaz’s own prayer (2:12) and asks him to become its answer, and she bases her appeal not on her worth but on who he is: “you are a redeemer”. It is the way every sinner may come to Christ.

3.reflection:
Naomi seeks “rest” for Ruth (v. 1), and the chapter ends with Ruth waiting while Boaz will not rest (v. 18). What does it mean for you to rest in Christ because he is working on your behalf?

Ruth appeals to Boaz on the ground of who he is, “for you are a redeemer” (v. 9), not of what she deserves. Why is that the only ground on which we can come to Christ? How does it free us when we feel unworthy?

Alone at night, Boaz responds with blessing, honour and restraint, and then protects Ruth’s reputation (vv. 10–14). What does his example teach about purity and about guarding the good name of others when no one is watching?

Boaz will not bypass the nearer redeemer, even at the risk of losing Ruth (vv. 12–13). Where are you tempted to get a good thing by cutting corners? What would doing it God’s way cost you, and why is it worth it?

4.title: The Redeemer Steps Forward

So they sat down.<sup>3</sup>Then he said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech.<sup>4</sup>So I thought I would tell you of it and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem,<sup>12</sup>and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring that the LORD will give you by this young woman."<sup>13</sup>So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son.<sup>14</sup>Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel!<sup>15</sup>He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."<sup>16</sup>Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse.<sup>17</sup>And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.<sup>18</sup>Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,<sup>19</sup>Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,<sup>20</sup>Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,<sup>21</sup>Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,<sup>22</sup>Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
4.overview:
Where we are. Boaz has sworn to redeem Ruth, and Naomi has said he will not rest until the matter is settled (3:18). Chapter 4 is the book’s last scene, redeemed. It moves from the threshing floor to the city gate, and from a village wedding to the cradle of David.

The message. The LORD provides a redeemer who is willing to pay the cost, and through him fills the empty with life. The nearer kinsman has the right but will not risk his own inheritance; Boaz pays the price, marries Ruth and keeps the dead man’s name alive. Then the LORD gives a son, the women bless the LORD “who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (v. 14), and the genealogy shows that God has been building the house of David all along.

Why it was said. The first readers lived under David’s house (see the introduction). The chapter tells them where their king came from: a redemption done openly and lawfully, a Moabite welcomed into Israel by faith, and a child given by the LORD. David’s throne rested on God’s loyal love, not on a spotless pedigree.

How the chapter makes its case. At the gate, before ten elders, the nearer redeemer agrees to buy Elimelech’s land, then withdraws when he learns that he must also take Ruth and raise up an heir for the dead (vv. 1–6). A sandal seals the transfer; Boaz declares before witnesses that he has bought the land and taken Ruth “to perpetuate the name of the dead”, and the people bless the marriage by Rachel, Leah and the house of Perez (vv. 7–12). The LORD gives Ruth a son; the women bless the LORD, Naomi holds the child, and he is named Obed, the grandfather of David (vv. 13–17). A ten-name genealogy from Perez to David closes the book (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by family line and by pattern. Matthew writes “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” into the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), so this village wedding is a link in the chain that leads to the Son of David born in Bethlehem. And Boaz’s willingness to be impaired for others is a faint likeness of the Redeemer who, “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and who bought his people “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

For us. God’s hidden providence was building something far bigger than two widows could see, and he is doing the same through your ordinary faithfulness. Thank him for the Redeemer who counted the cost and paid it; then stop guarding yourself, and spend yourself for others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the city gate, the nearer redeemer shows that having the right to redeem is not the same as being willing. Boaz sits at the gate, stops the kinsman as he passes, and gathers ten elders as witnesses (vv. 1–2). He offers him the first right to buy back Elimelech’s land from Naomi, and the man agrees at once (vv. 3–4). Then Boaz names the condition: whoever buys the field takes Ruth the Moabite as well, to raise up an heir in the dead man’s name who will inherit the land (v. 5). Unwilling to damage his own inheritance, the man withdraws and hands his right to Boaz (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption requires not only right and resources but willingness. The nearer kinsman has the legal right and presumably the resources, but when the full cost is revealed, he will not pay it.
verseByVerse.examples: The nearer kinsman is the prudent, calculating man who weighs the cost of redemption against his own interest and finds it too high. He is not wicked; he is simply unwilling to be diminished for another's sake, and his 'I cannot... lest I impair my own inheritance' is the opposite of the gospel’s self-giving love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. And behold, the redeemer, of whom Boaz had spoken, came by. So Boaz said, "Turn aside, friend; sit down here." And he turned aside and sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz goes straight to the city gate, the place of public business, and the very redeemer he needs comes by.

Now Boaz had gone up to the gate and sat down there. True to Naomi’s word (3:18). The city gate was the town’s public square, where elders heard cases and business was witnessed (Deuteronomy 21:19). Boaz does everything openly, before witnesses.

And behold, the redeemer… came by. Again “behold” signals providence: the right man passes at the right moment, as Ruth “happened” upon the right field (2:3).

Turn aside, friend. The man is left unnamed. He would not preserve the name of the dead, and his own name is not preserved, while Boaz and Ruth are remembered for ever. A quiet justice runs through it.

Uncertain wording. “Friend” renders peloni almoni, an expression like “so-and-so”, used elsewhere for a place left unnamed (1 Samuel 21:2; 2 Kings 6:8). Boaz surely called the man by name; the narrator, it seems, chose not to record it.
verseByVerse.note: The city gate was the place of public business and law.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took ten men of the elders of the city and said, "Sit down here." So they sat down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz gathers ten elders as witnesses, so that the redemption will be public, lawful and beyond dispute.

Ten men of the elders of the city. The elders were the leading men of the town, who witnessed and judged important matters. Ten may have been a customary number for such a hearing; later Jewish practice required ten men for certain public acts.

Done in the open. Boaz cuts no corners. Ruth’s redemption must be beyond challenge, so that her marriage and her child will be fully legitimate. His care over legal form is itself a kind of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. So I thought I would tell you of it and say, 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me, that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I come after you." And he said, "I will redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz tells the nearer redeemer that Naomi is selling Elimelech’s land and offers him the first right to redeem it; seeing only a field, he agrees.

The parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech. Boaz begins with the land, not with Ruth. Israel’s land belonged to the LORD and was held by families as their inheritance; when poverty forced a sale, the nearest kinsman had the right and duty to buy it back so that it stayed in the clan (Leviticus 25:23–25). We are not told how the widow came to be selling it, or exactly what was being sold, perhaps the right to the land and its crops; the point is that it must be redeemed within the family.

I come after you. Boaz honours the man’s prior claim. He could have schemed around him, but his integrity will not allow it.

I will redeem it. Hearing only of the land, a profitable addition to his holdings, the kinsman agrees at once. Boaz has let him commit himself before he hears the full cost, and true redemption is about to cost more than he is willing to pay.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said, "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz names the condition: whoever buys the field also takes Ruth, the widow, to raise up an heir who will carry the dead man’s name and inherit the land.

You also acquire Ruth the Moabite. The redemption of land (Leviticus 25) here meets the purpose of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10): the redeemer must marry Ruth and raise up a son who will carry Mahlon’s name and inherit his property, so continuing Elimelech’s line. And once more she is “Ruth the Moabite”, the outsider’s label persisting to the end.

A changed transaction. The land would no longer be a lasting addition to the redeemer’s estate. The son born to Ruth would inherit it as the heir of the dead. The redeemer would pay the price, support Ruth and the child, and then see the land pass out of his own line.

How the levirate law applies. The levirate law applied to a dead man’s brother. Here its purpose, to preserve the dead man’s name and inheritance, is carried to the nearest kinsman, along with the redemption of the land.

The cost of redemption. Redemption that costs nothing is no redemption at all. The true price is about to expose the difference between a redeemer who calculates and a redeemer who loves.

Textual note. The standard Hebrew text reads “you also buy it from Ruth the Moabite” (as the ESV notes in its margin). Most translations read “you also acquire Ruth”, which fits Boaz’s own words in verse 10. Either way, the field and the widow go together, and that is the point of the verse.
verseByVerse.note: The Masoretic Text reads “you also buy it from Ruth” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself, for I cannot redeem it." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nearer redeemer withdraws, unwilling to damage his own inheritance, and hands his right to Boaz.

I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance. His reasoning is self-protective: raising an heir for the dead would diminish his own inheritance and complicate his family’s. He is not portrayed as wicked, merely prudent and unwilling to be diminished for another’s sake. He gives up his claim and steps out of the story for ever, nameless.

A picture of the law? Many preachers have drawn a lesson from this moment, though the text itself does not, so it is best offered as an application: the nameless kinsman as a picture of the law. The law has a prior and rightful claim on us, for we are lawbreakers and its demand is just. But it cannot set us free without giving up its own just demands. The law can condemn; it cannot save.

From “I cannot” to “I will”. When the nearer redeemer steps back, another steps forward, willing to bear the full cost himself. Boaz’s willingness points beyond him to the one who was willing to be impaired, indeed made poor, that we might be made rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and who said, “I lay down my life for the sheep” (John 10:15).

The safety of the unspent heart. The nearer kinsman would fit comfortably into our world. He is not cruel. He protects his inheritance, keeps his commitments manageable, and does not let anyone’s need cost him too much. We have a whole vocabulary for this now, some of it wise: boundaries, self-care, protecting your peace. But a life organised around never being impaired has a hidden price. C. S. Lewis warned, in The Four Loves, that to love at all is to be vulnerable, and that a heart locked safely away where nothing can reach it will not be broken; it will become unbreakable, which is far worse. The kinsman kept his estate intact and lost his name. Boaz spent himself and stands in the line of Christ. Jesus made it a law of his kingdom: “whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25). And he did not only say it. He is the Redeemer who was willing to be impaired for us, and people who know they were bought at that price find the courage to stop guarding themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Boaz redeems openly, and the town blesses what he has done. The narrator explains the old custom by which a man sealed a transfer by handing over his sandal, and the nearer redeemer does so (vv. 7–8). Boaz declares before the elders and all the people that he has bought everything that belonged to Elimelech and his sons, and taken Ruth the Moabite as his wife, so that the dead man’s name will not be cut off (vv. 9–10). The people answer as witnesses and pray that Ruth will be like Rachel and Leah, that Boaz will prosper, and that his house will be like the house of Perez (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who bears the full cost gladly. The sandal ceremony (Deut 25:9) and the public declaration make the redemption legally complete and witnessed. The blessing sets this redemption within God's covenant purposes leading to David and the Messiah.
verseByVerse.examples: Boaz models the willing redeemer who counts the beloved worth every cost. The community's blessing reminds us that redemption and marriage are matters of covenant community, witnessed and celebrated by the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this was the custom in former times in Israel concerning redeeming and exchanging: to confirm a transaction, the one drew off his sandal and gave it to the other, and this was the manner of attesting in Israel. So when the redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself," he drew off his sandal. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator explains an old custom: the nearer redeemer seals the transfer of his right by drawing off his sandal and handing it to Boaz.

Now this was the custom in former times in Israel. The narrator explains it for later readers, a sign that the book was written some time after the events (see the introduction). To confirm a transfer, one man drew off his sandal and gave it to the other: a public, binding gesture, a kind of ancient signature.

An echo of Deuteronomy. In Deuteronomy 25:9 a widow pulled off the sandal of a brother-in-law who refused his duty, and spat in his face, to shame him. Here there is no shaming; the gesture is simply a formal handing over of the right to redeem.

He drew off his sandal. With that, Ruth’s redemption is no shadowy arrangement but a fully witnessed, formally sealed transfer. The transaction that leads to David, and to David’s greater Son, is sealed with the removal of a shoe in a village gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Boaz said to the elders and all the people, "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon. Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have bought to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place. You are witnesses this day." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz declares before the elders and the people that he has bought Elimelech’s land and taken Ruth as his wife, so that the dead man’s name will not be cut off.

You are witnesses this day. The whole community is called to witness, and the phrase frames the declaration at its beginning and its end.

Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon. Only here do we learn which son Ruth had married. Where the nearer kinsman recoiled at the cost, Boaz embraces it, and the crown of his declaration is not the land but Ruth.

That the name of the dead may not be cut off. He acts not for gain but to preserve a dead kinsman’s line, fill Naomi’s empty house and give Ruth a home.

A name for one who had none. The gospel pattern shines here: the willing redeemer pays the full price to make the destitute his own. Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25); he has bought his bride at infinite cost, given her his name, and brought life where there was only the cutting off of death. As we read, we are witnesses to a redemption that pictures our own.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people who were at the gate and the elders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman, who is coming into your house, like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel. May you act worthily in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem, and may your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the offspring that the LORD will give you by this young woman." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people and elders bless the marriage, praying that Ruth will be like Rachel and Leah, that Boaz will prosper, and that his house will be like the house of Perez.

We are witnesses. The whole gate answers, and its threefold blessing ties this village marriage into the whole story of God’s people.

Like Rachel and Leah. Rachel and Leah “together built up the house of Israel”. To liken a Moabite to the mothers of the nation is a stunning affirmation of her full inclusion.

May you act worthily in Ephrathah. Strength, worth and a good name for Boaz in his own town.

Like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah. Most remarkable of all. Tamar, like Ruth, was a childless widow who, by very irregular means (Genesis 38), secured an heir for the line of Judah, and bore Perez, Boaz’s own ancestor (v. 18). God has often advanced his purposes through unlikely women and tangled circumstances, and the mention of Perez prepares for the genealogy that closes the book.

Outsiders in the line of Christ. Tamar (probably a Canaanite), Rahab and Ruth all stand in Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3–5), monuments to the grace of a God who delights to bring the outsider in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — The Redeemer's Son and the Line of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD gives a son, and the emptied woman is filled. Boaz marries Ruth, and the LORD gives her conception (v. 13). The women of Bethlehem bless the LORD, who has not left Naomi without a redeemer, and call the child the restorer of her life, born of a daughter-in-law who is worth more to her than seven sons (vv. 14–15). Naomi takes the child into her lap; the neighbours say, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and name him Obed. Only then does the narrator reveal who he is: the father of Jesse, the father of David (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The reader hears in v. 13 the familiar note of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah: life as God's gift, not a human achievement. And the closing genealogy reveals the hidden providence of the whole book as God's plan to bring forth the messianic king.
verseByVerse.examples: Naomi, who returned empty and bitter, now holds a grandchild to her bosom, the proof that God's providence was for her all along. The women's praise of Ruth as 'more to you than seven sons' honors the foreign daughter-in-law above what that culture counted the highest blessing. No act of loyal love is wasted with God. And for readers whose arms are still empty: the LORD who gave Ruth a son does not give every longed-for child, and childlessness is never a mark of his disfavour. Naomi’s deepest gift was not finally a baby but a Redeemer, and that gift is offered to every believer, with a place in Christ’s own family that no loss can take away (Mark 3:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boaz marries Ruth, and the LORD gives her a son: the hidden God is named as the giver of life.

So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. In a single verse the redemption is completed and the pledge of the threshing floor is kept.

The LORD gave her conception. The narrator could simply have said that Ruth conceived; instead he names the LORD, only the second time he has done so in his own voice (1:6). Ruth had been married to Mahlon for some years in Moab without a child (1:4–5).

The hidden God named. The God who seemed hidden throughout, who worked behind the coincidences and never spoke, is named as the giver of life. Ruth’s loyalty, Naomi’s plan and Boaz’s redemption were his instruments; the child is his gift, for “children are a heritage from the LORD” (Psalm 127:3).

What it does not mean. This is not a promise that every childless couple will conceive. It is a testimony that life is God’s gift, and that he fills empty lives in many ways, as he filled Naomi’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel! He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women of Bethlehem bless the LORD for giving Naomi a redeemer in this child, who will restore her life and sustain her old age, born of a daughter-in-law worth more than seven sons.

Then the women said to Naomi. The women who asked “Is this Naomi?” (1:19) now gather to bless her, completing the great reversal of the book.

Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer. Naomi said the LORD had dealt bitterly with her; the women praise him for not leaving her without a redeemer. Here the redeemer is most immediately the child, the heir who will secure her future, though the words also take in what Boaz has done.

A restorer of life. Literally “one who brings back life”, using the verb “return” that ran through chapter 1. The woman who came back empty is brought back to life.

More to you than seven sons. In a culture that prized sons above all, with seven the number of completeness (1 Samuel 2:5), this is the highest possible praise, and it is given to the Moabite “who loves you”. The bitter woman is blessed, and the God she accused has redeemed her beyond all her hopes.

Uncertain wording. In “may his name be renowned in Israel” the Hebrew could refer to the LORD or to the child. Most take it of the child, whose name has indeed been remembered, as David’s grandfather.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse. And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naomi takes the child into her lap, the neighbours say, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and name him Obed; then the narrator reveals that he was David’s grandfather.

Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap. The woman who said “the LORD has brought me back empty” now holds a child. “Became his nurse” means she cared for him and helped to raise him. The empty arms are full at last.

A son has been born to Naomi. Through Ruth’s son the line of Elimelech, which seemed extinguished in the deaths of chapter 1, goes on. The bitterness of chapter 1 is answered by the blessing of chapter 4.

They named him Obed. The name means “servant”, probably short for “servant of the LORD”.

He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. The genealogical climax, saved for the last word. David, the king to whom God promised an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16), traces his ancestry through this child, through Boaz the redeemer and Ruth the Moabite. God was never merely arranging the comfort of two widows; he was forging a link in the chain that leads to the throne of David and beyond it, to the manger.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse's family stayed in Bethlehem, where Samuel would find David (1 Sam 16:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — The Genealogy: From Perez to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book closes by setting a village story inside the history of salvation. A ten-name genealogy runs from Perez, Judah’s son by Tamar, through Boaz the redeemer, to Obed, Jesse and finally David (vv. 18–22). The list is short and probably selective, but its point is plain: the famine, the funerals, the vow on the road, the chance field, the night at the threshing floor and the redemption at the gate were all part of God’s hidden work to give Israel its king. Matthew carries the same line on to Jesus (Matthew 1:5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogy unlocks the book's purpose. The story of Ruth is not merely a beautiful tale of loyalty and redemption; it is part of the messianic line. The list from Perez to David sets the redemption of a Moabite widow within God’s promise that the ruler would come from Judah (Gen 49:10). The hidden providence of the whole book is revealed as God's purpose to bring forth the Son of David, the King of kings.
verseByVerse.examples: God works across generations, weaving individual lives of faith into purposes that span centuries. Ruth and Boaz could not see that their loyal love would lead to David and to Christ; they simply acted faithfully in their moment. So we may be faithful in our own small stories, trusting that God is weaving them into a design we cannot yet see. The smallest acts of hesed echo into eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends with ten generations from Perez to David, showing that this village story was part of God’s plan to give Israel its king and, through him, to bless the world.

Now these are the generations of Perez. The phrase is the heading Genesis uses for its family histories, and it sets the story of Ruth within the great story of God’s people. Perez is Judah’s son by Tamar, named in the people’s blessing (v. 12); ten names later comes David.

A selective list. Ten names cover several centuries, so the list probably skips generations, as biblical genealogies often do. Matthew names Rahab as Boaz’s mother (Matthew 1:5): an outsider’s son married an outsider, and both are in the line of Christ.

For the first readers. The book was probably written under the monarchy, when David’s house ruled (it explains old customs for a later generation; see the note on vv. 7–8). For those readers it answered a question they may well have asked: how could Israel’s king have a Moabite great-grandmother, from a people the law kept out of the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:3)? The book’s answer is that Ruth came in by faith, taking refuge under the LORD’s wings (2:12), and that David’s house stood on the LORD’s hesed, not on a spotless pedigree. David seems to have remembered the link: when Saul hunted him, he sheltered his parents with the king of Moab (1 Samuel 22:3–4).

Where the story was heading. Everything has been building towards this. The famine, the funerals, the vow on the road from Moab, the “chance” arrival in Boaz’s field, the bold request at the threshing floor, the willing redeemer at the gate and the child given by the LORD were all God’s hidden work to bring forth David, the king who received the promise of an everlasting throne (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

From the barley fields to the manger. The New Testament carries the line one decisive step further: Matthew sets Ruth the Moabite in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the Son of David (Matthew 1:5–6). The story of a destitute foreign widow and a worthy redeemer leads from the barley fields of Bethlehem to the manger of Bethlehem, from gleaning grain to the one who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The God who seemed absent and silent through the suffering was weaving redemption all along, not only for Naomi and Ruth, but for the world.

4.theology:
The Willing Redeemer and the Law That Cannot Save. The nearer redeemer has the right and resources but lacks the willingness: 'I cannot redeem it, lest I impair my own inheritance' (v. 6). Many have seen in him a picture of the law, which has a just claim on us but cannot redeem (Rom 8:3); the text does not say so, and the application is fair only if held lightly. Boaz steps forward as the willing redeemer who gladly bears the full cost. So Christ, the eternal Son with every right and infinite resources, was supremely willing to be 'impaired' (to become poor, to bear our sin, to bear the law's curse) that we might be redeemed.

The God Who Fills the Empty. The God who seemed hidden is named in v. 13 as the giver of life, and the woman who returned 'empty' holds a child to her bosom (v. 16). This is Romans 8:28 told as a story: God working all things, even the deaths and the emptiness, for the good of those who love him and are called according to his purpose.

Grace to the Outsider in the Line of the Messiah. Ruth the Moabite, labeled by her foreignness to the very end, stands in the genealogy that leads to David and, through Matthew 1:5, to Jesus Christ. Alongside Tamar and Rahab, she foreshadows the gospel that will reach every nation.
4.examples:
Then: The transaction at the gate reflects ancient Israel's legal customs: the elders as witnesses, land redemption (Lev 25:25) intertwined with levirate marriage (Deut 25:5–10), and the sandal that sealed the transfer. Redemption and marriage were matters for the whole community of God’s people, not merely private arrangements.

Now: Boaz confronts us with the question every redeemer faces: is the beloved worth the cost? We can answer as he did only because we have first been answered: Christ counted us worth his own life, and his Spirit now makes self-giving love possible where calculation once ruled. And the closing genealogy teaches us to live faithfully in our own small stories, trusting that God weaves them into purposes that span generations. Naomi could not see, in her bitterness, that her empty arms would one day cradle the ancestor of the Messiah. So we trust the God of hidden providence, who fills the empty, redeems the outsider, and brings forth from our ordinary faithfulness a glory we cannot yet imagine.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel!
keyVerse.note: The women’s blessing turns Naomi’s lament (1:20–21) into praise and names the theme of the whole book: the LORD does not leave his people without a redeemer. The child in Naomi’s lap is the grandfather of David, and the line runs on to the Redeemer God has given to all who trust him.

4.reflection:
The nearer redeemer had the right to redeem but would not “impair my own inheritance” (v. 6). Where are you most tempted to protect yourself from the cost of loving someone? What would it look like to be willing to be “impaired” for another’s good?

Boaz did everything openly, before witnesses and in proper order (vv. 1–2, 9–10). Why does integrity in the public and practical side of life matter for Christians, and where might it be tested for you?

The women bless the LORD, “who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (v. 14). Look back over the whole book: where did God seem absent, and where was he actually at work? How does that help you read your own story?

The book ends with a genealogy leading to David (vv. 18–22), and Matthew carries it on to Jesus. How does it encourage you that God wove a Moabite widow, a grieving woman and an ordinary farmer into the line of Christ? What might he be doing with your ordinary faithfulness?
